title: What My Father Taught Me About Learning Slowly
script: Narrator: [warmly] My father never finished secondary school. He started working at fourteen, and books were never really part of his life.
Narrator: [thoughtful] When I was young, I sometimes felt embarrassed that he couldn't help me with my homework the way other fathers could.
Narrator: [reflective] But at fifty, something surprising happened. My father decided to learn how to read English, slowly, using an old phrasebook.
Narrator: [gently] Every evening after dinner, he sat at the table with that small book, moving his finger slowly under each line.
Narrator: [honestly] At first, I thought it was a strange hobby for a man his age, something that would not last more than a week.
Narrator: [softly] Months passed, and he kept going, one page some nights, sometimes just a few words on tired nights.
Narrator: [warmly] I asked him once why he was doing this so late in life. He said, learning late is still learning, my son.
Narrator: [thoughtful] He told me he simply wanted to read the labels on medicine bottles without asking anyone for help.
Narrator: [with feeling] That small, humble goal stayed with me. He was not trying to become fluent, just a little more capable.
Narrator: [reflective] Watching him struggle patiently with simple words taught me something my own classes never had.
Narrator: [gently] I used to give up quickly when something felt hard, closing the book after only a few frustrating minutes.
Narrator: [warmly] Now, when I study something difficult, I think of my father's finger moving slowly under those English words.
Narrator: [determined] I remind myself that slow progress is still progress, and starting late is still better than never starting.
Narrator: [peacefully] My father can now read simple instructions on his own, something that once felt completely out of reach for him.
Narrator: [with a small smile] He is not fluent, and he never wanted to be. He just wanted to understand a little more than yesterday.
Narrator: [warmly] That, I think, is the quietest and truest kind of education, the kind nobody grades but changes you completely.
